source.title: Actions Speak Louder than Words: Trillion-Parameter Sequential Transducers for Generative Recommendations
source.authors: Jiaqi Zhai; Lucy Liao; Xing Liu; Yueming Wang; Rui Li; Xuan Cao; Leon Gao; Zhaojie Gong; Fangda Gu; Michael He; Yin-Hua Lu; Yu Shi

record.tranche_reason: Tests compute-scaling in a new setting: generative recommendation models trained on user-action sequences, rather than language models trained on text.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling-sweep outcomes for recommendation metrics in Figure 7 and describes their trends in Section 4.3.1. Other architecture comparisons and results about stochastic sequence length do not test the claim versions recorded here.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own compute-scaling sweeps of recommendation models trained on user-action sequences (Figure 7, Section 4.3.1). This bears on whether a scaling-law form carries over to a non-text modality (V5). It does not measure language-model pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. The authors claim that GR retrieval metrics (HR@100, HR@500) and ranking NE empirically scale as a power law of training compute across three orders of magnitude, 'given appropriate hyperparameters', up to roughly GPT-3/LLaMa-2 compute. They say DLRMs plateau, though DLRMs may win at low compute. They present this as the first evidence that LLM-style scaling laws apply to large-scale recommendation.
record.recipe_differences: Recommendation models trained on user-action sequences; evaluation uses recommendation metrics versus compute, rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says exact model hyperparameters play a lesser role within a reasonable range, but sequence length is more important for GR scaling and should be increased alongside other parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors say sequence length matters much more for GRs than in language modeling and must be scaled together with other parameters. They also say exact hyperparameters matter less than total compute within a reasonable range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In generative recommenders, sequence length is a primary scaling axis, unlike in language models.

record.problems: The scaling results are for recommendation metrics, not language-model held-out cross-entropy. Figure 7 provides plotted sweeps and fitted expressions but no uncertainty estimates. The largest-run compute is normalized over 365 days for a streaming-training setting; exact DLRM configurations are withheld for confidentiality.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-sweep metrics were reported separately in the text beyond the three Figure 7 metrics for GRs and DLRMs.

untested.parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs; no held-out extrapolation is reported.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and data.
Effect of shape at fixed parameter count in language models. The paper only remarks that hyperparameters matter less than total compute, for recommenders.
Image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. Parameter-count and data-count scaling laws in recommenders are not fitted; only compute is.
Downstream performance of language models versus scale or loss.
Sensitivity of the exponents to fitting choices, and bending of curves away from a single power law.

missing.what: Parameter scaling: GRs keep scaling with embedding and non-embedding parameters up to 1.5 trillion parameters, whereas DLRMs saturate at about 200 billion parameters.
DLRMs may outperform GRs in the low-compute regime, which would make the curves cross.

record.verdict_notes: The record omits that the plotted fits are logarithmic in compute rather than power laws. Hit rate is a task metric, not a loss; NE is a normalized cross-entropy. Compute is normalized per year of streaming training. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict substantially larger runs.
The compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and how its components grow with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The paper tests recommendation models and training compute, not image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream performance related to language-model pretraining scale or pretraining loss; the reported metrics are recommendation-task metrics.
Whether exponents or compute-optimal allocation change with fitting choices or setup, and whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Generative Recommenders (GRs)
rows.size_stated: Scaling sweep; largest tested models had 8,192 sequence length, 1,024 embedding dimension, and 24 HSTU layers.
rows.operation_detail: Scaled GR configurations by adjusting model and sequence hyperparameters; plotted evaluation metrics against training compute.

conditions.value: Training PetaFLOPs per day; sweep across three orders of magnitude

rows.measure: Evaluation Hit Rate@100 versus training compute
rows.note: The plotted fit is given in the figure. The authors state that retrieval and ranking metrics empirically scale as a power law of compute across three orders of magnitude.
rows.check: The value is the plotted fit L = .15 + .0195 ln C, which is log-linear in compute, not a power law, although the authors call it one. The metric is retrieval hit rate, not a held-out loss. No uncertainty is given. The 'L' label is the paper's own.

source_check.correct: state: partial; HR@100 improves with compute, but the reported fit is log-linear and does not establish V5's power-law form.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 7, top panel, p. 9; Section 4.3.1, pp. 8–9.
source_check.problem: Observed overstates support for V5: systematic improvement alone does not establish the specified functional form.
